interactions.summary: After a student adds that the third case inspires the least imagination, Jiang folds the ranking exercise back into his master frame: lust is fantasy-escape, and Inferno should now be read as prophecy, meaning social critique rather than mere afterlife description.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student observation absorbed into Jiang lecture

interactions.summary: Jiang argues that Dante comes to be seen as a prophet because the Black Death makes his condemnations look like divine judgment, which then creates the paradox of how an all-loving God can also seem to threaten catastrophe.

speaker_notes.note: The student prompt is short but important because it links Jiang's lust argument to imagination, one of his central primitives.

claims.claim: Jiang says the worst lust case inspires the least imagination and therefore most completely abandons the life of faith, hope, and love.
Francesca is condemned because she escapes into fantasy rather than acting on real love for a real person.
Jiang distinguishes Paradiso from Inferno by saying Paradiso is vision or revelation, while Inferno is prophecy understood as social critique rather than fortune-telling.
Jiang frames the next part of the course as reading Inferno to understand Dante's criticism of Florentine society and to test whether those criticisms apply to the present.
Jiang argues that the Black Death helped later readers interpret Dante as a prophet whose denunciations anticipated divine judgment.
Jiang says prophetic anger comes from seeing disaster coming in advance, which is why biblical prophets and Dante sound furious rather than merely informative.
The Black Death creates a paradox for Jiang's reading because Dante's God is all-loving and merciful, yet the poem seems to promise catastrophic retribution.

signature_moments.moment: Inferno stops being fortune-telling and becomes a weapon of social criticism.
signature_moments.source_phrase: prophecy is a critique of the present
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the hinge that lets Jiang read Dante politically rather than as a museum piece about the afterlife.

signature_moments.moment: The Black Death retroactively turns Dante from strange poet into credible prophet.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this convinces everyone that dante is a prophet
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It explains how historical catastrophe changes the reception of a text into revelation and judgment.

signature_moments.moment: Prophets are angry because they already know the blow is coming.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: Jiang turns prophetic rage into a function of foresight rather than mere moralism.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's label for Paradiso as revelation of what the world and future should look like.
Not fortune-telling but a social critique that warns present society of judgment.

chronology_notes.note: Jiang dates Dante's death to 1321 and treats the later Black Death as the historical event that shifts readers into taking the poem as prophetic judgment.

uncertainty_notes.note: The transcript becomes noisy while Jiang improvises around dates and catastrophe, but the main claim is stable: later disaster makes Dante's curse look prophetic.
